label: thm:prime-main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:prime-main}
Let $F=\mathbb F_p$ be a field of prime order in which $-1$ is not a square, and let $P_3=\{(\underline x,\underline x\cdot \underline x):\underline x\in F^{2}\}$. Then $R^*(2\to r)\lesssim_r1$ for every
\[
r>\frac{176}{51}=3.45098\ldots .
\]
head: environment

label: thm:six-main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:six-main}
Let $F$ be a finite field of odd characteristic and let $P_6=\{(\xi,\xi\cdot \xi):\xi\in F^5\}\subset F^6$. Then
\[
R^*\Big(2\to\frac83\Big)\lesssim1,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
\|(f d\sigma)^\vee\|_{L^{8/3}(F^6)}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^2(P_6,d\sigma)}.
\]

label: eq:directional-low-high-split
title: Proof
body_md:
We may enlarge $\mathcal L$ to the family of all lines meeting $A$ in at most $C m^{1/2}$ points, since every ordered pair of distinct points determines a unique line and all terms are nonnegative. Constants in this proof may depend on $C$. Put $\mu=\min(m,p)$ and $\tau=\mu^{1/3}$. Split this family as
\[
\mathcal L=\mathcal L^-\sqcup\mathcal L^+,
\]
where the lines in $\mathcal L^-$ meet $A$ in at most $\tau$ points and those in $\mathcal L^+$ meet $A$ in more than $\tau$ points. Since
\[
E_{\theta,\mathcal L}(A)
=E_{\theta,\mathcal L^-}(A)+E_{\theta,\mathcal L^+}(A),
\]
the elementary inequality $(u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:directional-low-high-split}
\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L}(A)^2
\le 2\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L^-}(A)^2
 +2\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L^+}(A)^2.
\end{equation}

We first bound the low-richness part. In a fixed direction, the lines of $\mathcal L^-$ are parallel and disjoint. If such a line contains $r\le\tau$ points of $A$, then it contributes $r(r-1)\le\tau r$ ordered pairs. Consequently,
\[
E_{\theta,\mathcal L^-}(A)\le\tau m.
\]
Moreover, every ordered pair of distinct points has a unique direction, so
$\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L^-}(A)\le m^2$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:low-rich}
\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L^-}(A)^2
\le \tau m\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L^-}(A)
\le \tau m^3=m^3\mu^{1/3}.
\end{equation}

It remains to estimate $\mathcal L^+$. For dyadic parameters $j$ and $s$, let $\mathcal C_{j,s}$ be the lines in $\mathcal L^+$ meeting $A$ in between $j$ and $2j$ points and whose direction contains between $s$ and $2s$ such lines. The nonempty classes form a collection $\mathscr C$ of cardinality $J=O((1+\log m)^2)$. For each direction,
\[
E_{\theta,\mathcal L^+}(A)=\sum_{\mathcal C\in\mathscr C}E_{\theta,\mathcal C}(A),
\]
and Cauchy--Schwarz over the classes gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:class-cross-terms}
\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L^+}(A)^2
\le J\sum_{\mathcal C\in\mathscr C}
       \sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal C}(A)^2.
\end{equation}
Thus it is enough to prove the asserted bound uniformly for one class. More explicitly, if every class contributes at most $H$, then the right side of \eqref{eq:class-cross-terms} is at most $J^2H$. Since $J=O((1+\log m)^2)$, this costs at most $O((1+\log m)^4)$, which is absorbed into $p^\varepsilon$ because $m\le p^2$.

Fix a nonempty class $\mathcal C=\mathcal C_{j,s}$, and let $t$ be the number of directions it spans. Then $j\gtrsim\tau$, the class contains $\sim s$ lines in each of these directions and $\sim ts$ lines in all, and each line contains $\sim j$ points of $A$. For a fixed direction the class contributes $O(sj^2)$ ordered pairs, and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:class-energy}
\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal C}(A)^2\lesssim t(sj^2)^2=ts^2j^4.
\end{equation}
We will use three constraints repeatedly. There are $p+1$ directions, so $t\lesssim p$; the lines of one direction are parallel and disjoint, so $sj\lesssim m$; and the hypothesis gives $j\lesssim m^{1/2}$.

In this class each of the $\sim ts$ lines carries at least $j$ points, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:incidence-lower}
I(A,\mathcal C)\gtrsim jts.
\end{equation}
Whichever incidence bound applies, at least one term on its right side is $\gtrsim jts$. Suppose first that the class spans few directions, $t\le c_0p^2/m$, so that \eqref{eq:LPV} applies. If the term $t^{2/9}(ts)^{5/9}m^{7/9}$ in \eqref{eq:LPV} is $\gtrsim jts$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:LPV-class}
jts\lesssim t^{2/9}(ts)^{5/9}m^{7/9}\ \Longrightarrow\ t\lesssim m^{7/2}j^{-9/2}s^{-2}\ \Longrightarrow\ ts^2j^4\lesssim m^{7/2}j^{-1/2}.
\end{equation}
At the same time, Vinh's estimate \eqref{eq:vinh-inc} applies to this same class. If the term $mL/p\sim mts/p$ in \eqref{eq:vinh-inc} is $\gtrsim jts$, then $j\lesssim m/p$, and using $t\lesssim p$ and $sj\lesssim m$ gives
\[
ts^2j^4\lesssim p(m/j)^2j^4=pm^2j^2\lesssim \frac{m^4}{p}.
\]
If the term $(pmL)^{1/2}\sim(pmts)^{1/2}$ in \eqref{eq:vinh-inc} is $\gtrsim jts$, then $ts\lesssim pm/j^2$, and hence, using $sj\lesssim m$,
\[
ts^2j^4\lesssim (pmj^{-2})(mj^{-1})j^4=pm^2j.
\]
Consequently, in the case where the term $t^{2/9}(ts)^{5/9}m^{7/9}$ in \eqref{eq:LPV} is $\gtrsim jts$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:LPV-vinh-combined}
ts^2j^4\lesssim \frac{m^4}{p}+\min\{m^{7/2}j^{-1/2},\,pm^2j\}.
\end{equation}
If $m\le p$, then $j\gtrsim\mu^{1/3}=m^{1/3}$ and the minimum in \eqref{eq:LPV-vinh-combined} is $\lesssim m^{10/3}=m^3\mu^{1/3}$. If $m\ge p$, put $j_0=mp^{-2/3}$. Since $j_0\ge p^{1/3}=\mu^{1/3}$, either $j\le j_0$, in which case $pm^2j\le m^3p^{1/3}$, or $j\ge j_0$, in which case $m^{7/2}j^{-1/2}\le m^3p^{1/3}$. Thus this case contributes at most a constant multiple of
\[
\frac{m^4}{p}+m^3\mu^{1/3}.
\]

We next handle the other terms in \eqref{eq:LPV}. If the term $t^{1/2}(ts)^{1/2}m^{1/2}$ is $\gtrsim jts$, then $s\lesssim m/j^2$, so $ts^2j^4\lesssim tm^2\lesssim pm^2$. If the term $(ts)^{2/3}m^{2/3}$ is $\gtrsim jts$, then $ts\lesssim m^2j^{-3}$, so $ts^2j^4\lesssim m^2(sj)\lesssim m^3\le m^3\mu^{1/3}$. If the term $m$ is $\gtrsim jts$, then $ts^2j^4=(jts)(sj^3)\lesssim m^3\le m^3\mu^{1/3}$, using $sj\lesssim m$ and $j\lesssim m^{1/2}$. Finally, the $L$ term in \eqref{eq:LPV} satisfies $L\sim ts$ for the present class. If this term is $\gtrsim jts$, then $j\lesssim1$; using $sj\lesssim m$ and $t\lesssim p$ gives $ts^2j^4\lesssim ts^2\lesssim t(m/j)^2\lesssim pm^2$. Thus each class with few directions satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:few-dir}
ts^2j^4\lesssim m^3\mu^{1/3}+\frac{m^4}{p}+pm^2.
\end{equation}

Suppose instead that the class spans many directions, $t>c_0p^2/m$, which is outside the stated range of \eqref{eq:LPV}. Here \eqref{eq:vinh-inc} applies with $L\sim ts$, and by \eqref{eq:incidence-lower} one of its two terms is $\gtrsim jts$. If the term $mL/p\sim mts/p$ is $\gtrsim jts$, then $j\lesssim m/p$, so using $t\lesssim p$ and $sj\lesssim m$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:many-dir}
ts^2j^4\lesssim p(m/j)^2j^4=pm^2j^2\lesssim \frac{m^4}{p}.
\end{equation}
If the term $(pmL)^{1/2}\sim(pmts)^{1/2}$ is $\gtrsim jts$, then $ts\lesssim pm/j^2$, hence $s\lesssim m^2/(pj^2)$ by $t>c_0p^2/m$, and again $ts^2j^4\lesssim p\big(m^2/(pj^2)\big)^2j^4=m^4/p$.

The estimate \eqref{eq:few-dir} or \eqref{eq:many-dir} bounds \eqref{eq:class-energy} uniformly for every class. Summing over the classes in \eqref{eq:class-cross-terms}, combining with \eqref{eq:low-rich} and \eqref{eq:directional-low-high-split}, and absorbing the resulting $O((1+\log m)^4)$ factor into $p^\varepsilon$ gives \eqref{eq:dir-energy}.

label: prop:prime-B
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $k_*=m^{2/3}p^{-1/3}$ and $\mu=\min(m,p)$.

If $A$ and $B$ are $k$-regular with $k\le k_*$, then \eqref{eq:reg-R} gives $\mathcal R(A),\mathcal R(B)\lesssim m^2k$, so the second term of \eqref{eq:B-def} already gives the result,
\[
\mathcal B(A,B)\le p\big(\mathcal R(A)\mathcal R(B)\big)^{1/2}\lesssim pm^2k\le pm^2k_*=m^{8/3}p^{2/3}.
\]

Suppose instead that $A$ and $B$ are $k$-regular with $k\ge k_*$, and use the first term of \eqref{eq:B-def}, $\mathcal B(A,B)\le\mathcal T(A,B)=\sum_\theta E_\theta(A)E_\theta(B)$. Call a pair of distinct points a frame pair if the two points lie on a common frame line and a non-frame pair otherwise, and let $F_\theta(A)$ and $E_{\theta,\mathcal L_A}(A)$ count, respectively, the frame and non-frame pairs of $A$ of direction $\theta$, where $\mathcal L_A$ is the family of non-frame lines of $A$. Then $E_\theta(A)=F_\theta(A)+E_{\theta,\mathcal L_A}(A)$, and likewise for $B$, so expanding the product splits the trapezoid count into three parts,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:three-parts}
\mathcal T(A,B)=\sum_\theta F_\theta(A)F_\theta(B)+\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L_A}(A)E_{\theta,\mathcal L_B}(B)+\sum_\theta\big(F_\theta(A)E_{\theta,\mathcal L_B}(B)+E_{\theta,\mathcal L_A}(A)F_\theta(B)\big),
\end{equation}
the frame, non-frame, and mixed contributions, which we bound in turn. The non-frame lines $\mathcal L_A$ and $\mathcal L_B$ meet their sets in $O(k)=O(m^{1/2})$ points.

We record carefully the number of frame pairs. Write the regular decomposition of $A$ as
\[
A=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{r}A_i,\qquad A_i\subset\ell_i,
\qquad r\sim k,\qquad |A_i|\sim m/k,
\]
where the frame lines $\ell_i$ are distinct. For a fixed $i$, each set $A_j$ with $j\ne i$ contributes at most one point to $\ell_i$, because two distinct lines meet in at most one point. Hence
\[
|A\cap\ell_i|\le |A_i|+O(k)
\lesssim \frac{m}{k}+k
\lesssim \frac{m}{k},
\]
where the last inequality uses $k\le m^{1/2}$. A distinct pair lies on at most one frame line, and therefore
\[
\sum_\theta F_\theta(A)
\le \sum_{i=1}^{r}|A\cap\ell_i|^2
\lesssim k\left(\frac{m}{k}\right)^2
=\frac{m^2}{k}.
\]
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:frame-energy}
\Big(\sum_\theta F_\theta(A)^2\Big)^{1/2}
\le\sum_\theta F_\theta(A)
\lesssim\frac{m^2}{k},
\end{equation}
and likewise for $B$.

For the frame contribution, Cauchy--Schwarz in $\theta$ and \eqref{eq:frame-energy} give
\[
\sum_\theta F_\theta(A)F_\theta(B)\le\Big(\sum_\theta F_\theta(A)^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big(\sum_\theta F_\theta(B)^2\Big)^{1/2}\lesssim\frac{m^4}{k^2}\le\frac{m^4}{k_*^2}=m^{8/3}p^{2/3}.
\]
For the non-frame contribution, Lemma \ref{lem:directional-energy} applied to $(A,\mathcal L_A)$ and to $(B,\mathcal L_B)$ and Cauchy--Schwarz in $\theta$ give
\[
\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L_A}(A)E_{\theta,\mathcal L_B}(B)\le\Big(\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L_A}(A)^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big(\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L_B}(B)^2\Big)^{1/2}\lesssim_\varepsilon p^\varepsilon\Big(m^3\mu^{1/3}+\frac{m^4}{p}+pm^2\Big).
\]
For the mixed contribution, combining \eqref{eq:frame-energy} with the bound of Lemma \ref{lem:directional-energy} for $(B,\mathcal L_B)$ in the form
\[
\Big(\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L_B}(B)^2\Big)^{1/2}\lesssim_\varepsilon p^\varepsilon\Big(m^{3/2}\mu^{1/6}+m^2p^{-1/2}+p^{1/2}m\Big)
\]
through Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mixed}
\sum_\theta F_\theta(A)E_{\theta,\mathcal L_B}(B)
\lesssim_\varepsilon p^\varepsilon\,\frac{m^2}{k}\Big(m^{3/2}\mu^{1/6}+m^2p^{-1/2}+p^{1/2}m\Big).
\end{equation}
Using $k\ge k_*=m^{2/3}p^{-1/3}$, the three summands in \eqref{eq:mixed} are at most
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mixed-bounds}
m^{17/6}p^{1/3}\mu^{1/6},\qquad m^{10/3}p^{-1/6},\qquad m^{7/3}p^{5/6},
\end{equation}
respectively, and each is dominated by the right side of \eqref{eq:prime-B}. For the first term, if $m\le p$ it is $m^3p^{1/3}\le m^{8/3}p^{2/3}$, while if $m\ge p$ it is at most $m^3p^{1/3}=m^3\mu^{1/3}$. For the second term, if $m\le p$ it is at most $m^{10/3}=m^3\mu^{1/3}$; if $p\le m\le p^{3/2}$ it is at most $m^3p^{1/3}=m^3\mu^{1/3}$; and if $m\ge p^{3/2}$ it is at most $m^4/p$. For the third term, $m^{7/3}p^{5/6}\le m^{8/3}p^{2/3}+pm^2$ according as $m\ge p^{1/2}$ or $m\le p^{1/2}$. The other mixed term, with the roles of $A$ and $B$ exchanged, is identical. Combining the three contributions gives \eqref{eq:prime-B} for regular sets.

Finally, suppose that $A$ and $B$ are irregular. Let $\mathcal L$ be the family of all lines in $\mathbb F_p^2$. Since every line meets $A$ and $B$ in at most $m^{1/2}$ points, Lemma \ref{lem:directional-energy} applies to both $(A,\mathcal L)$ and $(B,\mathcal L)$. Also, because $\mathcal L$ is the family of all lines, every nonzero pair of points of $A$ or $B$ is counted in exactly one line of $\mathcal L$. Thus
\[
\mathcal T(A,B)
=
\sum_\theta E_\theta(A)E_\theta(B)
=
\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L}(A)E_{\theta,\mathcal L}(B).
\]
By Cauchy--Schwarz in $\theta$ and Lemma \ref{lem:directional-energy},
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal T(A,B)
&\le
\Big(\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L}(A)^2\Big)^{1/2}
\Big(\sum_\theta E_{\theta,\mathcal L}(B)^2\Big)^{1/2} \\
&\lesssim_\varepsilon
p^\varepsilon\Big(m^3\mu^{1/3}+\frac{m^4}{p}+pm^2\Big),
\end{aligned}
\]
where we used $|A|\sim|B|\sim m$ in the last line. Since $\mathcal B(A,B)\le\mathcal T(A,B)$, this proves the irregular case.

label: cor:hybrid-B
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:hybrid-B}
Suppose that $-1$ is not a square in $\mathbb F_p$. Let $A,B\subset\mathbb F_p^2$ be $k$-regular sets, or both irregular sets, with $|A|\sim|B|\sim m$ and
\[
m\lesssim p^{10/7}.
\]
Then, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hybrid-B}
\mathcal B(A,B)\lesssim_\varepsilon p^\varepsilon\left(
m^{8/3}p^{2/3}+\frac{m^4}{p}+pm^2+
\min\{m^3p^{1/3},\,m^2p^{10/7}\}\right).
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition \ref{prop:prime-B}, together with $\min(m,p)^{1/3}\le p^{1/3}$, gives the right side of \eqref{eq:hybrid-B} with $m^3p^{1/3}$ in place of the minimum.  Lemma \ref{lem:hybrid-rectangle} and the second alternative in \eqref{eq:B-def} give independently
\[
\mathcal B(A,B)\le p\big(\mathcal R(A)\mathcal R(B)\big)^{1/2}
\lesssim_\varepsilon p^\varepsilon m^2p^{10/7}.
\]
For nonnegative $U,V,D$ one has $\min\{U+V,D\}\le U+\min\{V,D\}$.  Applying this with
\[
U=m^{8/3}p^{2/3}+m^4p^{-1}+pm^2,
\qquad V=m^3p^{1/3},
\qquad D=m^2p^{10/7},
\]
proves the result.
